summary: I built SPHEREx Online, a free website that turns NASA's SPHEREx all-sky infrared survey into something anyone can explore and search for change. It shows the whole sky as a smooth, zoomable map in infrared colour, with a one-tap switch to visible light for comparison. When you tap "See changes here" on any spot, my site finds every SPHEREx image ever taken of it from my own index of all 1.6 million released SPHEREx images, downloads just that small patch, lines the images up and plays them as a flipbook. You get one frame per sky pass, a "difference" view where anything that moved or changed brightness stands out, and a colour view where cold objects such as brown dwarfs glow red. This is exactly how a hidden "Planet X" or a nearby cold brown dwarf would reveal itself: a faint red dot that moves between passes. The challenge test targets (Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, R Draconis and the Cat's Eye Nebula) are one tap away, and the flipbooks update themselves as NASA releases new data. No astronomy training, software or downloads are needed. It works in any browser, on a phone or a computer.
details:
What it does

SPHEREx Online lets anyone look for things that move or change in the sky using NASA's SPHEREx data:

  • Explore the whole sky. I show a full-screen, zoomable map of the sky in infrared (SPHEREx), either in colour (three infrared bands as red, green and blue, so cold and dusty things look red) or at a single chosen wavelength. A Visible/Infrared switch flips to the visible-light sky (the DSS2 photographic survey) for comparison, and a gentle nudge suggests it when the infrared view gets blurry up close.
  • Find a place. You can search by name ("Pleiades", "Proxima Centauri") or by coordinates, pick a suggestion, or use "Try these" to fly to the challenge test targets.
    • Passes: all images from each SPHEREx pass over the spot, stacked into one clean frame, in colour (4.4 to 5 µm as red, 1.6 to 2.4 µm as green, 0.75 to 1.1 µm as blue) or black-and-white.
    • Difference: each pass minus the first. Grey means no change; a black-and-white pair means something moved; white or black means it brightened or faded.
    • All: every single image in time order.
  • See motion across decades. For fast-moving stars I mark where the star sits in the 1990s visible-light photo and how far it has moved since. Barnard's Star, for example, has moved 6 arcminutes in 35 years, about one fifth of the Moon's width.
  • Share and embed. Every view has its own link, and other sites can link straight to a spot: https://spherex.online/?ra=133.7598&dec=-7.2422&changes=1 opens that patch of sky with its flipbook (or ?target=barnard).
  • Type coordinates any common way: 08h55m10.831s -7d14m42.53s, 08 55 10.831 -07 14 42.53, 08:55:10.831 -07:14:42.53 or decimal degrees, with clear messages for out-of-range values.

How it works

  1. My own index of every SPHEREx image. NASA's search service was unreliable during the hackathon, so I built my own index from NASA's public AWS copy of the SPHEREx data. Instead of downloading the 65 MB images, I read only the first 22 KB or so of each file (its header) to learn where it points and when it was taken. Because SPHEREx's six detectors sit in a fixed layout, one header gives the footprints of all six. The result is 269,456 exposures × 6 detectors = 1,616,736 images (24 April 2025 to 5 October 2026, the full DR1 release plus the newest quick release), searchable for any point in the sky in milliseconds.
  2. Flipbook pipeline (Python). For a spot, my server looks up every covering image, downloads small cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA's cutout service in parallel, aligns them onto one grid (astropy and reproject), masks bad pixels, groups them into sky passes, median-stacks each pass and makes difference images. The colour version combines three detectors per pass with background removal, a noise-aware black point and an asinh stretch. A new spot takes about 20 seconds in black-and-white, with colour added about 25 seconds later.
  3. Always up to date. Each flipbook remembers how many images it used and the newest date. When you open one, the server checks my index (and NASA's live search when it is available) and rebuilds in the background if new images exist. The index itself refreshes from NASA's new data releases every day.
  4. Sky map. The colour infrared map is my own set of 16,381 map tiles built from IRSA's SPHEREx all-sky maps. The single-wavelength view streams NASA's SPHEREx spectral cube directly. Both are displayed with Aladin Lite (CDS).
  5. Hosting. Google Cloud Run (server), Google Cloud Storage (map tiles) and Cloudflare DNS, at https://spherex.online.

Accuracy

I checked every test target's position, motion and distance against SIMBAD, and all match exactly. I then measured each target in the actual SPHEREx images for every pass: all six sit within 2.5 arcseconds of where their motion predicts, which is less than half of one SPHEREx pixel (6.15 arcseconds). Note that the challenge's coordinates for WISE 0855 are its position around 2010; it moves 8.1 arcseconds a year, so my site places it at its 2026 position, 2.1 arcminutes away.

Benefits and what I hope to achieve

SPHEREx maps the entire sky every six months, which makes it a powerful tool for spotting moving and changing objects: nearby brown dwarfs, fast-moving stars, variable stars, and possibly an undiscovered planet in the outer Solar System. But today, seeing a single spot change over time takes specialist knowledge, catalogue searches, file downloads and analysis software. SPHEREx Online reduces that to one tap and makes it visual. I hope it lets students, citizen scientists and the public browse the infrared sky, understand how astronomers find moving objects, and maybe spot something new, and that it keeps growing with SPHEREx as NASA releases more data.

Tools and languages

Python (astropy, astropy-healpix, numpy, scipy, reproject, Pillow) for the data pipeline and server; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website (Aladin Lite v3 for the sky map); Google Cloud Run and Cloud Storage for hosting; NASA's AWS Open Data bucket and IRSA web services for data.

Limitations

The colour flipbooks are false-colour composites of three infrared bands, meant for spotting cold objects and changes, not for measuring brightness. SPHEREx pixels are 6 arcseconds, so the infrared view is softer than visible-light photos up close. A few passes lack blue-band images and are shown in black-and-white only.
